title: Pilgrimage: Vulture Peak
hookLine: the hill at Rajgir where many Mahayana sutras are set

lines: A STONE PATH IN THE DARK.
A BRICK LEDGE AT THE TOP.
cards: The path is stone, and it goes up. In the dark before sunrise, pilgrims climb it with flashlights, past boulders and scrub, breathing hard, stopping at small caves.
At the top there is no great temple: a low brick platform on a rocky ledge, a few lamps, some flowers, and a wide view over green hills just as the sky lightens.
Someone opens a small book and starts to chant, and the people around join in, low, against the wind. The hill is near the town of Rajgir in India, and in the old texts it has a strange name.

teach.b: First, the name. In Pali it's Gijjhakuta, vulture peak; some say the rocks at the top look like a vulture, folded and watching.
In the Buddha's day the town below was Rajagaha, a royal city, and the texts place him on this hill. Second, the old discourses.
The Great Discourse on the Final Passing, the one followed to Kushinagar yesterday, opens right here.

A king sends his chief minister up the path to ask the Buddha about going to war. The Buddha answers by talking about what keeps a people strong: meeting often, living in harmony, honoring their elders.
A hill for hard questions. Third, the Mahayana sutras. For Mahayana Buddhists, this hill is where the Buddha gave some of the teachings they treasure.
The Lotus Sutra opens on Vulture Peak, with a vast assembly gathered, and the longer form of the Heart Sutra is set here too.
So when Mahayana pilgrims chant at the top, they chant words that, in their tradition, were first heard on this very ledge. Fourth, a story Zen tells.
On Vulture Peak, it says, the Buddha once held up a flower and said nothing. Only one disciple, Mahakashyapa, smiled. Zen traces its line of teachers back to that smile.

The story is told in later Chinese Zen collections, such as the Gateless Gate, and Zen tells it as its own beginning. One hill holds the old discourses, the great Mahayana sutras, and a wordless flower.

how: Pilgrims climb the stone path to Vulture Peak near Rajgir, often before dawn, and chant sutras, offer lamps and flowers, or sit in meditation on the brick platform at the top.

games.q: you're the Buddha on Vulture Peak. a king's minister climbs up to ask whether his king should go to war. what do you do?
o: give the king a battle plan.
refuse to talk about kings at all.
talk about what keeps a people strong.
games.why: he talks about what keeps a people strong: meeting often, living in harmony, honoring elders. the answer goes under the question.

practice: If stairs are near and your body is up for it, climb a few slowly, feeling each foot lift, move and land; if not, lift each foot slowly in place while seated.
At the top, stop and stand still as if a view were opening in front of you, then sit and let your breath settle.

wordCard.voice: Pilgrimage. Going to the place to remember what happened there. On Vulture Peak, pilgrims climb to the ledge where the texts say the Buddha stayed and taught. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Gijjhakuta, Sanskrit Gridhrakuta: vulture peak, the hill above Rajagaha.

carryVoice: Your line: the hill of sutras. One ledge, and three ways of remembering it. Go gently.
